exp.0:9:
Paul asks Philemon for a favor on behalf of Onesimus, whom he calls "my son." The word "begotten" here is not literal: it means that Paul brought him to faith in Christ. "Bonds" refers to the chains of his imprisonment.

Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a fellow believer and his friend. Onesimus was a slave of Philemon who, according to the context, had left him and later came to know Paul. It is not known with certainty everything that happened, since the text gives no details. Paul could order Philemon what he should do, but he prefers to appeal to love. That is why he begins with tenderness, not with authority.

For today: when you need to correct someone or ask something of them, prefer love to pressure. And look at people with hope: God can change those others have given up on, and He calls us to receive them as brothers and sisters.
exp.0:20:
Paul tells Philemon that he wrote this letter confident that he will listen. He even believes Philemon will do more than he asks. Here "obedience" speaks of a willing response, not a military order. In the translation your reader uses, the word that means "even" appears in the verse as "also."

Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a fellow believer. He pleads with him to receive back Onesimus, a servant who had left him and who was now a brother in Christ. Paul offers to pay any debt. It is not known exactly what "more than I say" means: some think it hints at Onesimus's freedom, others that it is a general call to generosity.

For today: when you ask something of others, trust the best in them and make your request with respect. And if someone asks you for something right, respond with generosity, going beyond the minimum.
exp.0:5:
Here Paul prays that the sharing of Filemón's faith with others would be effective, or strong in its results. "Communication" means sharing or taking part, not only speaking. This grows as Filemón acknowledges all the good that God has already placed in his life through Christ. Some translators understand this as generosity and practical fellowship; others as sharing the gospel. Both ideas fit.

Paul writes from prison to his friend Filemón, a believer who helped the church. Before asking him something delicate about Onesimus, a slave who had run away, Paul commends his love and faith. In this way he prepares Filemón's heart with gratitude and affection.

For today: think about the good that God has placed in you and put it to use. Write down today one quality or gift God has given you, and share it with someone: a word of encouragement, a concrete help, or your testimony.
exp.0:24:
This verse closes the letter with a blessing: Paul wishes that the grace of Jesus Christ be with their spirit, that is, with their inner life. "Your" here is plural, so he is speaking to the whole church that met in Philemon's house. The final line, "Written from Rome to Philemon by Onesimus, a servant," is a note added in some ancient manuscripts; it is not part of what Paul wrote.

Paul writes as a prisoner, probably in Rome, though some think it may have been another city. The letter asks Philemon to receive Onesimus with love, his slave who had run away and who was now a believer. The greetings from Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke show that Paul was not alone.

For today: before looking for solutions to a conflict, ask for grace for yourself and for the other person. And remember to pray for those who serve alongside you, as Paul did.
exp.0:7:
Paul says that, because of the authority he has in Christ, he could give Philemon a command about what is right. The word "boldness" here means freedom or courage to speak with firmness; other versions say "complete freedom" or "confidence." Paul mentions his right to command, but makes it clear that he is not going to use it.

Paul writes from prison to his friend Philemon, a believer who had been kind to other Christians. Paul is about to ask him for something delicate: to take back Onesimus, a slave who had run away from him and who now believed in Christ. Before making the request, Paul praises Philemon's love and prepares the ground. The verses that follow show that he prefers to appeal to love rather than to authority.

Even when we have authority over someone, as parents, leaders, or teachers, we can choose to persuade with love instead of forcing. A humble request often touches the heart more than an order does.
exp.0:23:
Here Paul mentions four men who send greetings to Philemon: Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke. He calls them "my fellow workers," meaning companions who labor alongside him in the work of the gospel. The name "Demas" is simply the name of one of them.

Paul writes this letter from prison, probably in Rome, though some think of another place. He speaks to Philemon, a believer, about his slave Onesimus. At the end, Paul includes greetings from his team to show that he is not alone and that others support his request. Years later, in 2 Timothy 4:10, it is said that Demas deserted him, but here he still appears as a co-worker.

For today: serving God is best lived out as a team. Value those who serve alongside you, pray for them, and do not lose heart if someone fails; God still works through imperfect people.
exp.0:0:
Paul presents himself as a prisoner of Jesus Christ, together with his brother Timothy. He writes to Philemon, whom he calls "dearly beloved" and "fellow labourer." Paul does not say he is a prisoner of Rome, but of Christ, meaning that his life belongs to the Lord.

Paul writes this personal letter from prison. Tradition places his imprisonment in Rome, although some scholars have proposed other places, such as Ephesus. Philemon was a believer who, as far as can be seen, had a church meeting in his house. Paul greets him warmly before asking him for something delicate, which concerns the slave Onesimus.

Paul does not begin by giving orders, but by affirming friendship and shared work. Today we can imitate him: before correcting someone or asking a difficult favor, let us warmly acknowledge what is good in the other person. Sincere relationships open the door to more humble conversations.
exp.0:13:
Paul says he did not want to keep Onesimus without first asking Philemon. "Consent" here means agreement or permission. Paul wanted Philemon's help not to be forced, something done out of necessity, but given gladly, of his own free will. In other words, it should be a free act and not an obligation.

Paul writes from prison to his friend Philemon. Onesimus, a slave belonging to Philemon, had left him and later served Paul. Paul sends him back and asks that he be received with affection. Although Paul could have decided on his own or pressed Philemon, he prefers to respect Philemon's freedom and responsibility. The Bible does not detail everything that happened, so it is best not to assume more.

For today: when you ask someone for a favor or lead others, avoid pressuring or manipulating. Invite with respect and leave room for the other person to decide freely. And when someone asks something of you, give gladly and from the heart.
exp.0:3:
Paul says that he thanks God and that he always remembers Philemon when he prays.

The phrase "making mention" means remembering someone with affection and bringing them up before God. The word "always" shows that this was not a one-time thing but a steady habit.

Paul writes this letter from prison to Philemon, a believer who hosted a church in his home. Before asking him for a delicate favor about Onesimus, Paul begins with gratitude and affection. The verses that follow explain the reason: he has heard of Philemon's love and of his faith in Jesus and toward all the saints.

Today we can imitate Paul: before correcting someone or asking something of them, let us thank God for that person. Let us make a list of people we are thankful for and pray for them by name, consistently.
exp.0:4:
Paul says that he has heard about the love of Philemon, and about the faith he has in the Lord Jesus. That faith and love do not stay private: they reach "all the saints," that is, all believers in Christ.

Paul writes from prison to his friend Philemon, who led a church that met in his home. Later he will ask him to welcome Onesimus, a slave who had run away, with kindness. That is why Paul begins by recognizing Philemon's good character before making his request.

For today: true faith shows in how we treat people. Think of a brother or sister in the faith whom you can help or encourage this week, and do it with a concrete gesture.
exp.0:10:
Paul tells Philemon that Onesimus, who once was useless to him, is now useful to both of them. The explanation of the name is included here: Onesimus means "useful" or "profitable." This is a play on words.

Paul writes from prison to his friend Philemon. Onesimus had been a servant of Philemon who had run away from him, and it is known that Paul brought him to faith. Now Paul sends him back and asks that he be received warmly. Scholars do not agree on the exact details of how Onesimus left, since the text does not give them.

God can transform any person. For that reason, let us not define anyone only by their past. If someone has changed, let us give them a chance, and if we are the ones who have failed, let us remember that in Christ we can start over and be a blessing to others.
exp.0:17:
Paul asks Philemon that, if Onesimus has wronged him in any way or owes him anything, Philemon should put it on Paul's account. "Wronged" means that he caused him loss, and "put it on my account" means: I will take responsibility for paying it.

Paul writes from prison to his friend Philemon. Onesimus, a slave who had run away from his home, is now returning, and Paul calls him a beloved brother. We do not know for certain what he owed; some think of money or of lost work time, but the text does not make it clear. Paul pleads that Philemon receive him with grace.

For today: when a relationship is broken, we can be bridges of reconciliation. This may mean taking on part of the cost of a debt, an apology, or a conflict that is not our own, just as Christ bore what we owed.
exp.0:6:
Paul says that he had great joy and was encouraged by Philemon's love. Practical love is what the original's wording points to here. To be refreshed means to be revived and relieved. The heart, the deepest feelings of believers, is what the phrase about the bowels of the saints points to. The saints are the Christians, those set apart for God. Philemon had made many believers feel refreshed and comforted.

Paul writes this letter from prison, and he addresses it to Philemon, a believer who hosted a church in his home. Before asking a delicate favor of him, namely to welcome Onesimus kindly, Paul acknowledges the good that is already in him. In this way he prepares Philemon's heart with sincere affection.

For today: think of someone who serves with love and tell them clearly how they have encouraged others. A word of gratitude can renew strength, and your own practical love can also bring relief to those around you.
exp.0:12:
Paul says he would have liked to keep Onesimus with him, so that Onesimus could serve Paul in place of Philemon while Paul was in prison for the sake of the gospel. "Retained" means keeping him or letting him stay on. The "bonds" refers to the chains or the imprisonment.

Paul writes from prison to his friend Philemon. Onesimus, a slave of Philemon, had run away from him and now believed in Christ. Paul sends him back, but first he expresses how highly he values him. His wish is not a command: he suggests that Onesimus would have served as Philemon himself would have done. Scholars discuss the details of how Onesimus came to be with Paul, and the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: even when we have authority or influence, we can treat others with respect and not with pressure. Paul prefers to ask out of love rather than to impose. We can do the same, letting the goodness of others be free and willing.
exp.0:18:
Paul says that he himself is writing this promise with his own hand, as a firm commitment: "I will repay it." Then he adds, tactfully, that he does not want to remind Philemon that he even owes Paul his own self. The point of that phrase is that Philemon has a greater debt to Paul, probably a spiritual one.

Paul writes to Philemon about Onesimus, a slave who had run away from him and who now returns as a believer. Paul asks that Philemon receive him as a brother. Many understand Philemon's debt to be that he came to know the gospel through Paul, although the text does not explain this in detail.

Today we can imitate Paul: when someone has failed and wants to start again, let us help them with concrete actions, taking on part of the cost, and not only with words.
exp.0:21:
It says that Paul asks Philemon to have a guest room ready for him. "Lodging" is a place to stay. Paul hopes that God will grant him release from prison through their prayers. The phrase "I shall be given unto you" means "I will be allowed to return to you."

Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, although not all scholars are certain of the place. He is pleading on behalf of Onesimus, a slave who had run away and is now a believer. In announcing his possible visit, Paul shows affection and also makes clear that Philemon will answer for how he treats Onesimus.

For today: pray for others with expectation and recognize that God uses our prayers. Also, live in such a way that you would not be embarrassed if someone came to visit and saw how you treat others.
exp.0:11:
Paul tells Philemon that he is sending Onesimus back to him, and asks him to receive him with all affection. The word "bowels" speaks of the deepest part of affection, like saying "mine own heart." "I have sent again" means "I am returning him to you."

Paul writes from prison to his friend Philemon. Onesimus, who was probably a slave of Philemon, had been away from him, and there he met Paul and came to believe in Christ. Scholars debate the details of how he came to be separated from his master, but the letter makes clear that Paul pleads for him. Paul calls him "my son" and asks that he be treated with love.

Today we can learn to receive with grace someone who has failed us or whom we have failed. If Christ has changed someone, let us give that person a real opportunity, looking at them with the same affection with which God receives us.
exp.0:14:
Paul tells Philemon that perhaps Onesimus left him for a while with a greater purpose: that now he may receive him back forever. The word "perhaps" means "maybe," and "departed" refers to Onesimus having gone away. Paul does not claim with certainty that God planned it this way; he says it with caution.

Paul writes from prison to Philemon, his friend and fellow believer. Onesimus, Philemon's slave, had left, and later came to know Christ together with Paul. Now Paul sends him back and asks Philemon to receive him with love, as a brother in the faith.

For today: when a separation or a problem hurts you, ask God for eyes to see whether He can use it for good, without assuming you understand everything. And if someone who failed you comes back changed, consider receiving him with forgiveness and as a brother.
exp.0:15:
He says that Philemon should no longer receive Onesimus as a mere servant, but as something far better: a beloved brother. Paul loves him very much, but he says Philemon should love him even more. "In the flesh" refers to ordinary human life, and "in the Lord" to the faith they share. "Especially" is the meaning of the word here.

Paul writes from prison to his friend Philemon. Onesimus, a servant of Philemon, had run away, and later he met Paul and came to believe in Christ. Paul sends him back with this letter, and asks Philemon to receive him with grace. We do not know all the details of what happened, but Paul pleads with affection, without imposing.

Today we may ask ourselves whom we see for their mistake, their social class, or their past. In Christ, that person can be our brother or sister. Today we can treat someone with respect and forgiveness.
exp.0:19:
Paul asks Philemon: "Yes, brother, let me have this joy from you for the sake of the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ." The words for "let me have joy" are rendered here in a plain sense, meaning to be given delight and gladness by you.

Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a believer who had a slave named Onesimus, who had run away from him. Now Onesimus is a believer, and Paul asks that Philemon receive him with forgiveness and as a brother. He even offers to pay any debt.

Today we can learn to ask for and to give reconciliation with humility and affection. If someone has offended you, think about how the love of Christ can help you forgive and restore that relationship, without harshness and with a willing heart.
exp.0:2:
Paul wishes Philemon and the others to receive "grace" and "peace." Grace is the undeserved favor of God, and peace is well-being and calm both with God and with one another. Both come from "God our Father" and from the "Lord Jesus Christ."

Paul writes from prison, together with Timothy, to Philemon, to Apphia, to Archippus, and to the church that met in Philemon's house. This greeting introduces a personal letter, in which Paul will later plead on behalf of Onesimus. It was a common greeting in his letters, but here it also prepares the hearts of the readers for a delicate matter: reconciliation.

For today: before speaking with someone about a difficult matter, we can begin by wishing them well from the heart and asking God for his grace and peace for both of you.
exp.0:22:
Paul says that Epaphras sends greetings to Philemon. He calls him "my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus," meaning someone who is locked up together with him because of Christ. The word "prison" here is understood to mean captivity or confinement.

Paul writes this short letter to Philemon from jail, asking him to welcome Onesimus, a servant who had run away. At the end he passes along greetings from co-workers. Epaphras also appears in Colossians as a faithful servant of Christ from the same region. We do not know for certain whether he was literally imprisoned or whether Paul uses the expression more broadly, and opinions differ.

For today: value those who share the hardships of following Jesus with you. Encourage them, greet them, and pray for them, because no one should suffer alone.
exp.0:16:
Paul asks Philemon that, if he truly considers him a partner, that is, someone he shares faith and work with, he should welcome Onesimus just as he would welcome Paul himself.

Paul writes from prison. Onesimus was a servant of Philemon who had run away from him, and now Paul is sending him back. Scholars discuss the exact details of what happened, but the text shows that Paul pleads for him as for a brother in Christ, not as for a mere slave.

Today we can apply this by receiving with grace someone who has failed and seeks to return, treating him as a brother. Perhaps we will also be called to intercede for someone who needs a second chance.
exp.0:1:
Paul also greets Apphia, whom he calls "beloved," and Archippus, whom he calls "our fellow soldier," that is, someone who works alongside him in the struggle for the gospel. He also greets the church that meets in Philemon's house.

Paul writes from prison, together with Timothy, a personal letter to Philemon. Apphia and Archippus could have been family members or close co-workers of Philemon, although the Bible does not make this clear. By naming the church, Paul shows that the matter of the letter, which concerns Onesimus, also matters to the whole community.

For today: value those who serve alongside you and remember that faith is lived out in community. Open your home, or your time, to encourage others and so that conflicts may be resolved with love and mutual support.
exp.0:8:
Paul says that he prefers to ask Philemon out of love, rather than give him an order. He describes himself as "Paul the aged," and also as a prisoner of Jesus Christ. The word he uses for asking is simply "I beg you," so the request is made as a plea. Rather than commanding, he chooses to appeal. Some translators understand "aged" to mean an older man, while others understand it to mean an ambassador, because the Greek word is similar. For that reason there are two possible interpretations.

Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a believer who had a slave named Onesimus. Paul wants to plead on behalf of Onesimus, who is now a believer. Although he has authority as an apostle, he chooses to appeal to Philemon's affection and freedom.

For today: when you need to ask someone for something difficult, do not use pressure or your position. Speak with humility and love, and let the other person decide freely and from the heart.

sum.0: Paul, writing from prison, addresses his friend Philemon and thanks him for his love and faith. He gently urges Philemon to welcome back Onesimus, who had earlier left and was of no use to him, but who is now a beloved brother and useful. Paul offers to pay back any debt, and he trusts that Philemon will do even more than he asks.
